caption: Figure 1. Sample accounting and response-panel effects. (a) The cerebellum and hippocampus matrices contain 53 region libraries from 29 Source Name animals. (b) Points are mean gene-level log2 effects; bars are 95% percentile intervals from 1,000 animal bootstraps within label and age. All regions of a sampled animal remain together. Panel labels are inherited exploratory gene sets, not measured transcriptional time windows. Intervals are conditional on normalization and cohort exchangeability.

Figure 2. Panel effects before ground-derived transformation across 17 primary design contrasts. Numbers show mean log2 effects; an asterisk denotes BH q < 0.05 across all 232 panel tests, including metadata sensitivities. Positive effects follow the numerator in each row. Cb, cerebellum; Hip, hippocampus; HGC, habitat ground control; VGC, vivarium control. OSD-563, OSD-564 and OSD-612 are three regions of one RR-10 animal cohort, not independent missions. Glial and endothelial transcript abundance does not directly measure inflammation or barrier permeability. Six displayed panels are selected from the eight tested; all tests remain in the supplied tables. Age and, for pooled core contrasts, tissue nuisance adjustment are retained.

Figure 3. Count-model robustness and biological candidate sensitivity. (a) The 120 panel comparisons summarize 15 regional contrasts fitted using PyDESeq2; agreement is analytical robustness on the same observations, not independent replication. (b) Full and metadata-excluded hippocampal ISS-T flight contrasts for SRG and circadian panels. Circles are log-expression effects with 1,000-animal-bootstrap percentile intervals; hollow diamonds show mean unshrunk negative-binomial effects for the full data. q values use the complete 232-test panel family. Exclusions remove the older FLT ISS-T support; the full SRG result does not establish a region-specific mechanism.

Figure 4. Paired regional interactions. (a) Source Name matching identifies 24 RRRM-2 and 10 RR-10 cerebellum–hippocampus animal pairs. (b) All eight panel effects in primary regional contrasts; no test has q≤0.05 across the complete 104-test family, including sensitivities. (c) Individual SRG hippocampus-minus-cerebellum scores; outlined points identify metadata conflicts. (d) SRG regional flight coefficients with 2,000-animal-bootstrap percentile intervals and complete-family q values. The approximate three-way interaction uses 9,999 restricted-model wild draws. Metadata exclusion removes all older FLT ISS-T animals, reducing the sensitivity to younger-animal exposure support.

Figure 5. Bounded score geometry and joint uncertainty. (a) Unbounded score gain for all 15 aligned anchor–target geometries; the bounded operator has gain at most two. (b) Observed sensor-panel effect-energy removal for matched hippocampal recovery and the RR-23 shared-HGC comparison. (c) Observed outside-sensor energy removal and 500-bootstrap percentile intervals, refitting normalization, anchor and target on each resample. Shared RR-23 HGC animals are sampled once for both roles. Intervals remain conditional on the fixed initially retained gene universe and observational sampling assumptions; zero crossings and negative reductions are shown. A point estimate may lie outside a biased percentile interval. Energy removal does not measure biological recovery.

Figure 6. Ground-only prediction and correction holdouts. (a) Within-age sensor and whole-genome AUC; (b) outside-sensor expression prediction error relative to a training-fitted intercept/age baseline; (c) training loading gain; (d) held-out outside-sensor collection-contrast energy removal. Points are split medians and lines are 2.5th–97.5th split quantiles, not independent-sample confidence intervals. Core regions use all 81 age-balanced holdouts each; RR-23 uses 200 prespecified distinct splits. Filtering, normalization references, nuisance means and scores use training data only. Five nested-CV strengths are selected only within training animals. The 362 splits overlap and involve 30 unique ground source animals. Projection is excluded from disjoint-sensor prediction because it uses response genes in its score. Reliable sensor discrimination does not establish biological recovery.

Figure 7. Prediction and amplification in the original ground holdouts. (a–c) Every retained split MSE ratio for five representative estimators; horizontal marks show means. All nine initial comparison methods and the added constrained estimator remain in electronic tables. The 81, 81 and 200 splits overlap and arise from 30 unique ground animals, so dot counts do not indicate independent sample sizes. (d–f) Mean operator gain against mean MSE ratio; dashed horizontal lines mark nuisance-only prediction and vertical dotted lines mark gain two. Available Sensor31 coordinates, training-only preprocessing and nested tuning are shared. Ordinary ridge can improve prediction substantially while having high amplification. The clipped-ridge points use the same five-candidate grid as constrained fitting; initial wider-grid results remain in complete tables. Gains are conditional on the normalized retained gene coordinates.

Figure 8. External prediction after within-cohort refitting. Dots are complete held-out individual animals or pools; horizontal marks are equal-unit mean MSE ratios and open diamonds are pooled SSE ratios. Five representative methods are shown, with the clipped comparator using the matched five-candidate grid; all initial and matched-grid methods are exported. (a) OSD-202, 40 individual animals; baseline includes collection time and unloading. (b) OSD-352 RR-3, six individual animals. (c) OSD-374, eight two-animal pools. (d) OSD-611, ten primary two-hippocampus pools listed in NASA SampleTable. The latter three baselines are intercept-only. Each held-out unit is excluded from preprocessing and inner tuning. Prediction improves on average with the constrained algorithm in every setting, but unbounded methods sometimes predict better. External settings are not biological replications of a common exposure, and coefficients are not transported unchanged between cohorts. No naive fold-based confidence intervals are shown.

Figure 9. Ground-anchor sensitivity and transfer. Dots show the observed change in squared contrast coefficients outside the Sensor31 genes after genome-expression projection or ground-calibrated score subtraction. Lines show 95% percentile ranges from 200 ground-animal bootstraps within age and cohort, conditional on normalized counts and a fixed target. These ranges describe anchor uncertainty, not complete sampling intervals or calibrated gene-level inference. The within-OSD-525 evaluation shares nine HGC animals with its anchor and is displayed as such. Negative reductions are retained. Removing expression variation is not proof of removing confounding.

Figure 10. RR-23 disjoint-anchor partitions. Each of 126 partitions trains on four of nine HGC animals plus the same eight VGC animals, then evaluates the nine FLT animals against the remaining five HGC animals. Training and evaluation animals are disjoint within a partition. Partitions reuse the same cohort and do not constitute 126 independent validations. (a) Removing sensor effect energy does not ensure a reduction outside the sensor. (b) λ is derived from conditional OLS t probabilities and is a dispersion diagnostic, not a measure of biological truth or empirical false-positive rate.

Figure 11. Independent training–target Gaussian mechanism benchmark. Five scenarios each contain 200 independently generated datasets (1,000 datasets; 7,000 method rows including additional oracle-ground and partial-correction references in the supplement). Four operational methods are shown without target tuning. Translucent violins show the full repetition distributions where variable; points and bars are means ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors, not real-data confidence intervals. Biological FDP compares discoveries with the original biological coefficient vector and therefore differs from conditional statistical FDR under residual nuisance. Power and biological energy retention are undefined when no biological effects exist. Failure under overlapping biology or changed coupling is retained. The simulator is not a complete RNA-seq generative model. Panels show (a) effect RMSE, (b) biological FDP, (c) power and (d) known biological-vector energy retention.

Figure 12. Exploratory high-gain stress benchmark. All 16 combinations of true gain (8 or 12), training size (24 or 96), target size (24 or 48) and unchanged or flipped outside-sensor nuisance coupling are shown. Each uses 100 independent repetitions (1,600 datasets; 6,400 method rows). Known biology is supported outside Sensor31 and is preserved exactly by both score operators. Error bars are ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors. Bounding reduces worst score amplification under coupling reversal but leaves substantial nuisance, including under unchanged coupling; neither norm control nor exact sensor-null preservation establishes accurate biological recovery. Panels (a,c) show unchanged-coupling RMSE and biological FDP; (b,d) show their flipped-coupling counterparts. Translucent violins show the full 100-repetition distributions where variable; points are means.

Figure 13. Real-count-calibrated known-truth comparison. Seven scenarios have 100 independently generated datasets at each source-training size, n=8 (a,b) and n=24 (c,d), with target n=24. (a,c) Percentage change in mean outside-sensor biological-effect RMSE relative to unadjusted inference; lower is better. (b,d) Mean biological false discovery proportion at within-dataset BH 0.05 across all 600 genes; power is reported in complete tables and can be low. The 14 pipelines share counts and truth within each repetition. Methods below the white line use target information; ComBat and known-batch regression receive target batch labels, and starred RUVg methods receive oracle-known negative controls. ComBat with “+ batch” retains batch in downstream regression. PCA is a separate expression-factor comparator. No information-matched superiority claim is made. All 19,600 runs completed; repetition distributions, Monte Carlo errors, effect RMSE for all genes and every configuration are supplied. Near-zero RMSE changes for nested ridge reflect frequent selection of no outside-sensor prediction.

Supplementary Figure 1. Conservative regional gene reproducibility screen. A candidate must have the same effect direction in every constituent contrast and finite component Wald p values; its intersection–union p value is the maximum component p. Discordant or unavailable effects receive p=1. All 54,989 region–gene combinations enter one global BH and BY family. No gene survives either correction. Component comparisons come from the same negative-binomial fits and can share samples; concordant direction alone is not replication evidence. Ranked nominal candidates are explicitly exploratory.

Supplementary Figure 2. Count-derived QC and expression structure across all seven deposits. (a–g) PCA of the top 2,000 variable log-expression genes in each deposit; axes give variance fractions. Groups use deposited exposure/cohort design labels; older core animals are squares and location conflicts are outlined. (h) Descriptive multivariate condition partial R² after age terms where available. (i) Mitochondrial gene-count fractions for every collapsed animal–region observation. These fractions use gene-assigned counts and are not measures of RNA integrity, mitochondrial injury or causal exposure effects. PCA and R² are descriptive; no discovery family is inferred from them.

Supplementary Figure 3. Direct within-region flight by collection interactions. (a,b) Panel interaction estimates and stratified animal-bootstrap intervals for each region; the asterisk marks the one panel passing the complete 32-test BH family. (c) Gene coefficient agreement between normalized-log and count models. (d) Whole-animal age support in each design cell. The highlighted full-data interaction has wild p=0.000838 and q=0.026816; metadata-excluded q=0.786. The 499,999 restricted wild draws are approximate inference, and omitted effects are descriptive stability checks. Exclusions leave one older FLT ISS-T animal in hippocampus and none in cerebellum. A common additive age effect does not resolve interactions in an empty design cell.

Supplementary Figure 4. Fixed erythroid-associated marker context. (a,b) Fixed marker-score distributions for every primary animal in each region; lines show group medians. (c) All seven count-model marker interaction coefficients with Wald intervals; asterisks refer to the existing complete gene family. (d) Marker-score versus Circadian-panel residual association after full-design adjustment. Target-omitted correlations for individual marker transcripts are supplied in the tables. No new marker significance family was selected. Beta-globin interactions motivate a possible composition contribution but do not establish blood contamination, a cell source, or an erythroid fraction. The complete tables retain markers failing the global family and all metadata sensitivities.

Supplementary Figure 5. Independent finite-sample and prediction robustness. (a,b) Refitted age-restricted label null distributions and observed Sensor31 AUC in each core region. All 400 assignments enter each exact test; all 18 panel/comparator tests enter BH and BY adjustment. (c) Outside-sensor original-score prediction error by training-expression tertile across all held-out animals. Points are means and bars are 2.5th–97.5th overlapping-split ranges, not independent-sample confidence limits. Ratios compare prediction with the training-fitted intercept/age baseline. (d) Saturated-age regional Circadian estimates with HC3 normal intervals. No estimate passes BH across all 64 saturated estimands. Exact collection association does not establish causal nuisance or biological recovery.

Supplementary Figure 6. Expanded biological robustness. (a,b) Circadian flight-by-collection estimates in hippocampus and cerebellum under additive age, each age separately and equal-age averaging, before and after fixed erythroid-score adjustment. Lines are 95% stratified whole-animal percentile-bootstrap intervals from 2,000 draws. (c) Additional residual variance associated with the seven-marker score after the complete base design, for all eight panels. (d) Maximum relative coefficient change from every single-animal or single-gene omission in the full additive-age design; these are dependence summaries, not confidence intervals. Marker covariates do not identify contamination, cell fractions or causal mediation. All finite inferential tests share the new complete family of 1,047 probabilities; unavailable designs and uncertainty remain in the tables.

Supplementary Figure 7. Biological context comparisons. (a) All eight panels in independent RR-3 bulk Brain, with three flight and three ground animals; RIN sensitivities remain in complete tables. (b) All panel radiation-by-unloading interactions in Earth OSD-202 at each collection time and their equal-time average. (c) Earth hippocampal radiation effects, using pools as the inference units and NASA-retained primary Si28 pools. (d) Common-gene panel direction consistency across original same-anatomy flight contexts. Lines are 95% whole-unit percentile-bootstrap intervals from 2,000 draws. Consistent direction does not establish replicated significance: no screen passes the complete new family. Earth perturbations and bulk Brain are not equated with original regional flight effects. All dose comparisons, technical sensitivities, omission diagnostics and unavailable uncertainties are retained.
